One broken inheritance rarely hurts. Hundreds of them nobody reviews do.

In SharePoint, a library, folder or file inherits permissions from the site by default. Breaking that inheritance is quick and often well meant: one team needs access to one folder.

The cost shows up later. Every unique permission is an exception someone has to remember, review and clean up. That backlog is what the concept of permission debt describes, and it matters more once tools like Copilot surface whatever a user can technically reach.

The article covers how inheritance works, why breaking it adds up, and which native options you can try first, such as separate sites or sharing links for single items.

6.page:
Breaking permission inheritance in SharePoint is a fast fix with a long tail.

By default, content inherits permissions from the site. Once inheritance is broken, the item has unique permissions that no longer follow site-level changes. Each of these is an exception that needs a review process, or it stays in place long after the original need is gone.

That accumulated backlog of overly broad, inherited or outdated access is what the permission debt concept describes. It tends to stay latent until AI tools such as Copilot surface the data.

Access rarely becomes a problem in one big mistake. It becomes a problem through hundreds of small, reasonable decisions.

That is permission drift: access slowly diverges from business reality through role changes, leftover groups and exceptions nobody removes.

A useful way to think about it: compare what an identity has been granted with what it actually uses. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management calls this the Permission Creep Index, where a higher score means more unused, excessive permissions.

The counterweight is least privilege: the smallest role, at the smallest scope, for the shortest time that still gets the work done.

The article covers how drift happens, where to look for it and what to do about it, with a reminder to test any cleanup on a pilot first.
